scope

2026,2008]
1. Covers Scheduled Areas and
Scheduled Tribes in any State other than

2. Notified in 10 States - Andhra

1. Covers Tribal Areas in four north-eastern States
- Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, Mizoram - which are
NOT in the Fifth Schedule.
2. Ten autonomous councils, by State:
(a) Assam (3): Bodoland Territorial, Karbi Anglong,
Dima Hasao.
(b) Meghalaya (3): Khasi Hills, Jaintia Hills, Garo Hills.

Application of

Part IX, excluded by Art 243M, was extended

1. Part IX does not extend here; no PESA

2. No Panchayats; nomination here is to the
District or Regional Council.
Degree of
autonomy
1. Weak autonomy - the Governor and the
State dominate; the Tribes Advisory
Council only advises and has no veto.
2. The tribal voice is consultative and
protection is administered from above.
1. Strong autonomy - the Councils hold legislative,
executive, judicial and financial powers together, the
widest self government of any local body in India.
2. Some Councils, such as the Bodoland Territorial
Council, hold powers over a longer list of subjects
under separate accords.
Object and
criteria for
declaring an
area
[PRELIMS
2015]
1. Dhebar Commission criteria -
preponderance of tribal population,
compactness and reasonable size,
viability as an administrative entity,
economic backwardness.
2. The object is protection of the interests
of Scheduled Tribes - not boundary fixing,
and not determining the powers of
Panchayats.
1. The same object, pursued through self-governance
rather than protective regulation by the Governor.
Governing
body, nature
of powers and
Union control
[PRELIMS
2025]
1. The Governor, supervised by the
President - no autonomous council, no
separate legislative body; the Tribes
Advisory Council only advises.
2. The executive power of the State extends
to the Scheduled Areas; the State does not
lose it.
1. Autonomous District and Regional Councils under
the Governor - genuine units of self-government with
law-making power, not advisory bodies.
2. These areas too remain under the State's executive
authority.
3. No equivalent annual report to the President.
4. Union grants-in-aid for these areas (Art 275(1)).

3. The Governor reports annually, or when
required, to the President on their
administration (Para 3).
4. The Union's executive power extends only
to giving directions to the State; no
takeover of administration.
Declaration
and alteration
of areas
[PRELIMS
2023]
1. The President declares an area a
Scheduled Area by order and may
increase, decrease, rename or rescind it
(Para 6).
2. Done in consultation with the Governor.
1. The Governor creates, increases, decreases, renames
and dissolves autonomous districts, on a
Commission's recommendation.
2. No Presidential role.
Composition
of the
advisory or
governing
body
1. Tribes Advisory Council of up to 20
members, three-fourths of them
representatives of the Scheduled Tribes in
the State Legislative Assembly (Para 4).
2. It advises the Governor, who rules on its
membership and mode of appointment.
1. Autonomous District Council of not more than 30
members - up to 4 nominated by the Governor, 26
elected, for a five-year term.
2. Exception: the Bodoland Territorial Council may have
46 members - 40 elected, 6 nominated.
Legislative
powers
1. No direct law making power vests in the
tribal population; the State Legislature
legislates for a Scheduled Area in the
ordinary way.
2. The Governor may make regulations for
the peace and good government of the
area, with the President's assent (Para 5).
3. Such a regulation may repeal or amend an
Act of Parliament or of the State
legislature in its application to the area.
1. The Councils have real law making power, exercised
through Bills passed by the Council (Para 3).
2. Subjects: land other than reserved forest,
management of forests other than reserved forest,
shifting cultivation, village and town administration
including village police and public health, inheritance
of property, marriage and divorce, social customs.
3. Every such law takes effect only on the Governor's
assent (Para 3).
Governor's
role:
regulation
making and
protective
safeguards
[PRELIMS
2022,2019]
1. The Governor may make regulations,
requiring the President's assent, to
restrict transfer of land by or among
Scheduled Tribes and to regulate money
lending (Para 5).
2. Source of the power to declare a transfer
of tribal land, including for mining, null and
void.
3. The role is dominant: the Governor is the
custodian of Scheduled Areas and his
powers here are wider than anywhere else
in the Constitution.
1. Protection works through the Councils' own legislative
and judicial powers, not gubernatorial regulations.
2. The Governor's main role is to give assent to Council
laws and regulations (Para 3).
3. The Governor may alter or dissolve a Council, but day
to day powers rest with the Council.
Applicability
of Union and
State laws
1. An Act of Parliament or the State
legislature applies by default.
2. The Governor may direct that it shall not
apply, or apply with modifications (Para
5).
1. On matters within the Councils' competence, Acts of
Parliament or the State legislature do not apply of
their own force.
2. For other matters the Governor may direct
non-application or modified application.
Judicial
powers
1. None. The regular State judiciary and the
ordinary civil and criminal courts operate in
Scheduled Areas.
2. Customary law is protected, if at all,
through the Governor's regulations and
not through tribal courts.
1. The Councils may constitute village councils and
courts to try suits and cases between parties all of
whom belong to Scheduled Tribes of the area (Para 4).
2. They apply customary law; the Governor may confer
wider civil and criminal jurisdiction on them.
3. Appeals lie to the District Council and thereafter to the
High Court as the Governor specifies.

275(1))
Financial
powers
1. No financial autonomy - no separate fund
and no power of taxation; the
administration is financed through the
State machinery.
2. The Union may make grants in aid to the
State for tribal welfare and for raising the
level of administration of Scheduled Areas
(Art 275(1)).
1. The Councils may levy and collect land revenue, taxes
on lands and buildings, tolls, taxes on professions,
trades, animals, vehicles, entry of goods into a market
and for the maintenance of schools and roads (Para 8).
2. Each Council has its own District Fund or Regional
Fund (Para 7).
3. The Councils also receive grants in aid from the
Consolidated Fund of India (Art 275(1)).
4. The Councils may grant licences or leases for
extraction of minerals and share in royalties (Para 9).
EVOLUTION AND COMMITTEES
Evolution of local self government [PRELIMS 2009]
Rural committees
Committee (year) Focus Key recommendations
Balwant Rai Mehta (1957) Review of the Community
Development Programme
(1952) and National
Extension Service (1953)
Three tiers: Gram Panchayat, Panchayat Samiti, Zila Parishad. Samiti
executive; Zila Parishad advisory, headed by the Collector. Direct
elections at village level, indirect above. Core idea: democratic
decentralisation. First inaugurated by Nehru at Nagaur, Rajasthan (2
October 1959); Andhra Pradesh next.

#### K. Santhanam (1963) PRI finances Special taxes on land revenue and home tax; all grants consolidated
and released to PRIs; a Panchayati Raj Finance Corporation in each
State.
Ashok Mehta (1977 to 78) 132 recommendations Two tiers: Zila Parishad (executive) and Mandal Panchayat (15,000 to
20,000 people). District as the first point of decentralisation. Parties
contest openly; compulsory taxation; social audit; elections within six
months of supersession; Nyaya Panchayats; a State Minister for PR;
SC/ST reservation.
Dantwala (1978) Block level planning Block as the unit of planning; Collector central to district planning.
C.H. Hanumantha Rao
(1984)
District planning District Planning Bodies headed by the Collector or a Minister.
G.V.K. Rao (1985),
Planning Commission
Bureaucratisation of
development (“grass
without roots”)
Zila Parishad as pivot; planning shifted to the district; a District
Development Commissioner as CEO of the Zila Parishad; regular
elections.
L.M. Singhvi (1986) Constitutional recognition A new chapter in the Constitution; Gram Sabha as direct democracy;
viable village panchayats; Nyaya Panchayats; more finances; judicial
tribunals for election disputes.
Sarkaria Commission
(1988)
Centre State relations Regular elections to PRIs; no prolonged supersession.
P.K. Thungon (1988) Constitutional recognition Three tiers, Zila Parishad as pivot; five year term; supersession not
beyond six months; a subject list in the Constitution; reservation
including women; State Finance Commission; Collector as CEO of the
Zila Parishad.
Gadgil (1988) Constitutional status Three tiers; five year term; direct elections at all levels; reservation for
SCs, STs and women; planning and taxation powers; State Finance
Commission and State Election Commission. Basis for the 64th
Amendment Bill (1989), which shaped the 73rd Amendment (1992).
Sushil Kumar (2025),
MoPR
Proxy representation The “Sarpanch Pati” / “Pradhan Pati” problem; penalties for proxy
leadership; measures to empower elected women representatives.

Urban milestones
Year Milestone Significance
1688 Madras Municipal Corporation First municipal corporation; Bombay and Calcutta followed in 1726.
1870 Mayo’s Resolution Financial decentralisation begins.
1882 Ripon’s Resolution Magna Carta of local self government: largely elected boards with non
official chairmen; Ripon is the father of local self government.
1907 Royal Commission on Decentralisation
(Hobhouse)
Reviewed local bodies.
1919, 1935 GoI Acts 1919: a transferred subject under dyarchy. 1935: a provincial subject.
1949 to 1988 Urban committees Local Finance Enquiry (1949 to 51, P.K. Wattal); Taxation Enquiry
Commission (1953 to 54, John Matthai); Rural Urban Relationship
(1963 to 66, A.P. Jain); Financial Resources of ULBs (1963, Rafiq
Zakaria); Constitution, Powers and Laws of ULBs (1982, K.N. Sahaya);
National Commission on Urbanisation (1985 to 88, C.M. Correa).
1989 Rajiv Gandhi: 64th (Panchayats) and
65th (Nagarpalika) Amendment Bills
Passed the Lok Sabha, failed in the Rajya Sabha.
1990 V.P. Singh: a fresh Bill Lapsed with the government.
1991 to 92 Narasimha Rao Dropped the controversial features; the 73rd and 74th Amendment
Acts, 1992.
Traps: Ashok Mehta proposed two tiers; Balwant Rai Mehta, Thungon and Gadgil proposed three. G.V.K. Rao and Thungon
made the Zila Parishad the pivot; Ashok Mehta made the district the first point of decentralisation.
